concept.name: Spin-off
concept.definition: A corporate action in which a company separates a division into an independent company by distributing new shares in it to existing shareholders, generally pro rata. Holders end up owning shares in both the parent and the spun-off entity.
concept.intuition: A spin-off unbundles a conglomerate so each business can be managed - and valued - on its own merits.
concept.mechanics: The parent distributes the subsidiary's shares to its holders as a stock dividend, often structured to be tax-free; the new shares may first be offered through a rights issue to existing shareholders before being offered to new investors. On distribution the parent's price drops by the value of what was separated.
concept.failure_modes: Spin-offs can load debt or liabilities onto the smaller entity, both stocks often sell off initially as index funds and disinterested holders exit, and separation costs can exceed the hoped-for sum-of-the-parts uplift.
concept.misconceptions: Receiving spin-off shares is not a windfall: the parent's price falls by the value distributed, just as with a dividend, and spin-offs are not guaranteed to unlock value.
concept.example: When eBay spun off PayPal in 2015, each eBay shareholder received one PayPal share per eBay share held; the two separately priced companies together approximated eBay's prior market value.

citations.source: Investopedia, What Is a Corporate Action?
